item.title: Maruti Suzuki, Tata Motors PV, other auto stocks soar up to 7%; Nifty Auto index jumps 4%. What’s driving the rally?
item.description: Auto stocks, including Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, Maruti Suzuki and M&M, rallied on Thursday as copper, aluminium and other industrial metals slid to multi-month lows. The correction could ease raw-material cost pressures for automakers and support margins, although a stronger dollar and concerns over global demand drove the commodity sell-off.
item.dc:creator: Veer Sharma
item.content:encoded: Shares of automobile companies, including Tata Motors, Maruti Suzuki and M&M, rallied up to 7% on Thursday, lifting the Nifty Auto index by 4%. The gains came as aluminium, copper and other key metals used in the industry fell to a seven-month low, easing concerns over rising input costs.Maruti Suzuki, India’s largest carmaker, was the biggest gainer in the pack, surging over 6.5% to Rs 13,487 apiece on the BSE, while Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles gained 4%. M&M advanced 5% to Rs 3,508 per share. Hyundai Motor India shares also rose over 4% to Rs 2,193 apiece, while commercial vehicle maker Ashok Leyland climbed over 2%.Metal prices tumbleOn Wednesday, benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange (LME) fell for a fifth consecutive session, touching its lowest level since April 13, Reuters reported. Prices recovered marginally on Thursday.Also read: Japan stocks fall as metal shares slide; investors await Anthropic IPO debut The current move in LME copper prices looks more like relief than a decisive turn. The sharp retreat was driven by a buoyant US dollar and growing question marks over the pace of the AI data-center buildout, where copper is a key input in the infrastructure, Reuters cited Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. The main factors to watch remain the path of the dollar, any further signals on AI-related capital spending, and Chinese demand indicators. Further, aluminum hit a 51-month low, while tin prices plunged to an 8-month low.Domestic brokerage Emkay says the sell-off is primarily driven by a stronger US dollar and weakness in global equity markets, triggering widespread profit booking and long liquidation. Traders also appeared to reduce positions to manage mark-to-market (M2M) losses.Notably, Wednesday recorded the highest single-day trading volume compared with the average daily volumes of the previous month, indicating significant position unwinding and heightened market activity.Meanwhile, China's uneven economic recovery and concerns over demand from its construction and manufacturing sectors are weighing on sentiment, experts say.Higher crude oil prices have also influenced the outlook for industrial metals. Rising energy costs increase expenses across the mining, smelting, refining, and transportation chain. Aluminium and zinc, in particular, are highly sensitive to power costs.While higher costs can sometimes support commodity prices by constraining supply, markets are currently more focused on the risks to economic growth. Rising energy costs can curb business activity, industrial production and consumer spending, ultimately weakening demand for metals used in construction, machinery, infrastructure and automobiles.Read more: Base metals lose momentum amid strong dollar and demand concernsWhy could auto companies benefit?The decline in copper, aluminium and tin prices could provide relief to Indian automakers by lowering raw-material costs. These metals are used in vehicle manufacturing, electrical components, wiring, engines and other auto parts. Cheaper inputs can reduce production expenses and ease pressure on operating margins. Aluminium, copper, rubber, and plastic components account for 40-45% of passenger vehicle raw material costs.Foreign brokerage Jefferies said the earnings outlook for auto OEMs weakened in CY26 primarily due to the intense commodity cost rally. It added that the auto industry faces a high base of volumes starting 2HFY27 as commodity cost pressures continue, albeit at a lower intensity than seen in the first half of the financial year.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. item.title: Explained: Why United Breweries, Radico Khaitan, other liquor stocks tumbled up to 6% on Thursday
item.description: India's effective 162.5% duty on bulk Scotch imports has triggered a dispute under the India-UK trade pact, which had cut tariffs to 75%. The move has left more than 80 containers stranded at ports and raised concerns for domestic liquor makers that use imported Scotch in blended whisky production operations.
item.dc:creator: Veer Sharma
item.content:encoded: Shares of liquor makers, including United Breweries, Radico Khaitan, United Spirits and Allied Blenders tumbled up to 6% on Thursday as India is set to impose an effective duty of 162.5% on bulk Scotch imports. The levy is higher than the 150% tariff that applied before the India-UK trade agreement, according to a Reuters report. In today's session, Tilaknagar Industries tumbled 6%, while United Spirits slipped more than 3% after the opening bell. United Breweries, Allied Blenders, and Radico Khaitan edged lower by up to 2%.The India-UK trade pact, which came into effect on July 15, cut tariffs on Scotch whisky to 75%. The reduction was welcomed by both British authorities and businesses, particularly companies such as Pernod Ricard and Diageo, which import Scotch in bulk and blend it to produce popular brands for India's $65 billion liquor market.However, the tariff reduction has now triggered the first major dispute under the agreement. Indian investigators allege that companies have been using incorrect customs classifications for bulk Scotch concentrates, which are treated as raw materials in the production of blended whiskies and other alcoholic beverages.According to the investigators, imports of these concentrates have, since May, fallen under a newly introduced customs category for compound alcoholic preparations , which carries a tariff of 150%.An additional consumption tax takes the effective duty on these imports to 162.5%, according to a government document reviewed by Reuters and eight sources familiar with the matter, including industry executives and customs agents.The dispute has left thousands of litres of bulk Scotch stranded at Indian ports. More than 80 shipping containers belonging to Pernod, Diageo and Bacardi have been held up as the standoff continues, Reuters reported last week.The British government has repeatedly said it is engaging with New Delhi to resolve the issue, while the Indian government has indicated that the matter will be settled soon.In the meantime, Pernod and Diageo are arranging bank guarantees and other financing to secure the release of their detained shipments and keep operations running. Bacardi, meanwhile, is still weighing its options, three of the sources said.The scrutiny also extends to domestic liquor manufacturers. Mumbai-listed Radico Khaitan, Allied Blenders and Distillers, and Tilaknagar Industries import bulk Scotch and are facing the same customs concerns as Pernod and Diageo.For smaller companies, arranging bank guarantees could prove more challenging, particularly if collateral is required. Such guarantees must also be disclosed as contingent liabilities.Around 80% of Scotch whisky imported from Britain by volume enters India in bulk, making the country the world's largest Scotch market by volume.A large proportion of these imports is used to manufacture Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) whisky. The process involves blending relatively small quantities of Scotch with other spirits to produce mass-market whiskies, which are considerably cheaper than fully imported brands such as Chivas Regal and Johnnie Walker.Whisky tariffs had been among the contentious issues during the lengthy negotiations that preceded the trade agreement, which came into effect on July 15 to considerable celebration. Britain had said the pact would benefit several iconic UK products , including whiskies.The UK's Scotch Whisky Association has estimated that the trade agreement could increase Scotch exports to India by $1.34 billion over five years, according to a Reuters report.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser.
